title: Himachal on a budget: real costs for 2026
meta_description: What a budget trip to Himachal really costs in 2026: HRTC bus fares, hostel and homestay rates, dhaba meals and three sample trips from ₹12,000.
summary: A careful traveller can see Himachal for ₹1,800–3,000 a day by riding HRTC buses, sleeping in hostels, HPTDC rooms and family homestays, and eating at dhabas. A week in the Kullu valley or Dharamshala costs about ₹15,000–22,000 from Delhi, Kinnaur a little more. Here is where the money goes.

sections.heading: What a budget day costs
paras: Himachal is one of the cheapest Himalayan states to travel in, because the state bus network is dense and a whole economy of hostels, guesthouses and homestays has grown up around students and backpackers. The figures below are indicative 2026 ranges we see on the ground, per person, and they rise in peak weeks. Check current fares before you travel.

For most saver travellers the daily spend falls between ₹1,800 and ₹3,000. The lower end is a dorm bed, dhaba meals and one short bus ride. The upper end is a private double split between two, a café meal and a paid activity such as a guide or an entry ticket. The single biggest variable is where you sleep, followed by how often you take taxis instead of buses.

sections.heading: Getting there and around for less
paras: The Himachal Road Transport Corporation, HRTC, is the budget traveller's best friend. Its Volvo and semi-deluxe coaches leave Delhi's Kashmere Gate ISBT every evening for Shimla, Manali, Dharamshala and the Kullu valley, and its ordinary buses reach almost every village with a road. Book Volvo seats on the HRTC online portal rather than through agents, who often add ₹200–400 for the same seat.

Inside the hive, ordinary buses cost a fraction of taxis. Shimla to Manali by ordinary bus is roughly ₹450–650 against ₹5,000–7,000 for a taxi. Manali to Naggar is under ₹50. Even the long ride from Shimla to Reckong Peo in Kinnaur costs a few hundred rupees. The trade-off is time and comfort: buses stop often, can be crowded in the morning, and the last departure on rural routes may be early afternoon.

For Shimla, the Kalka–Shimla toy train is cheap in its ordinary second-class coaches, often under ₹100, and the views are the same as from the more expensive chair cars. Overnight trains reach Kalka, Chandigarh and Pathankot from Delhi, and sleeper fares on these trains can undercut the Volvo.
list: Book the Delhi Volvo 5–10 days ahead in season; weekend seats sell out.
Ask the conductor for the last bus back before you leave on a day trip.
Use shared taxis only where buses do not run, such as some Parvati valley stretches.

sections.heading: Where to sleep cheaply
paras: Hostels are now everywhere on the backpacker circuit: Old Manali, Kasol and Chalal, Bir, Dharamkot and McLeodganj all have dorms from about ₹500 and private rooms, and many have women-only dorms. Chains such as Zostel operate in Old Manali and Bir; check current listings for others before you book.

In Kinnaur, the Tirthan valley and smaller villages, family homestays are the better deal. A room with dinner and breakfast at ₹1,200–2,500 per person costs less than a guesthouse plus meals out, and the food is home-cooked. HPTDC, the state tourism corporation, runs dependable hotels in many towns, including Kalpa and Naggar Castle, at mid-range prices; their dorms and off-season discounts can be good value.

Rates swing hard with demand. The Christmas–New Year week and mid-May to June can double prices in Shimla and Manali. October and March are the sweet spots: good weather, fewer families on holiday, and room for bargaining on longer stays.

sections.heading: Eating well on a small budget
paras: Dhabas, the roadside and bazaar eateries, serve the same food Himachali families eat: rajma-chawal, kadhi, seasonal sabzi and rotis, usually ₹120–250 for a filling plate. In Kullu and Manali, look for siddu, a steamed wheat bun with a stuffing of walnut, poppy seed or lentil, eaten with ghee. In McLeodganj, Tibetan cafés serve momos and thukpa at prices students can manage.

Café menus in Kasol, Old Manali and Bhagsu are where budgets leak. A plate of shakshuka or pasta can cost ₹350–500, twice a dhaba meal. Eat one café meal a day if you enjoy them, and the other at a dhaba. In homestays, dinner is usually included and is the best food of the trip. Carry a steel bottle: many hostels and cafés refill water for free or for a small charge, which saves money and plastic.

sections.heading: Free and nearly free things to do
paras: Some of the best days in Himachal cost nothing beyond a bus ticket. The hot spring baths at Vashisht, across the river from Manali, are free and separated for men and women. The gurdwara at Manikaran, above Kasol, serves free langar to everyone, cooked partly in pots set into the hot springs; a donation is welcome but not required. In McLeodganj, the Lingkor circuit around the Tsuglagkhang is a quiet hour's walk among prayer flags and wheels, and the main temple has no entry fee.

Walking is the other great saver. From Old Manali, village paths lead up through apple orchards and deodar above the Manalsu stream. From Naggar, a lane climbs past the Roerich estate to the wooden Tripura Sundari temple. In Kinnaur, the cliff road from Kalpa to Roghi and the river walk from Sangla to Batseri cost only the effort. Shimla's Ridge and Mall, with Christ Church and the Gaiety Theatre, make a good half-day on foot.

Paid sights are mostly cheap. Museum and monument tickets such as the Bhuri Singh Museum in Chamba or the Roerich estate usually cost under ₹100 for Indian visitors; check current rates. Where money is well spent is a local guide for a trek, who adds safety and knowledge for ₹1,500–2,500 a day, shared across a group.

sections.heading: Where budgets go wrong
paras: Most overspending in Himachal is not about luxury. It is about time pressure, which pushes people into taxis, and about travelling in peak weeks, which pushes up room rates. A few habits keep a trip honest.
list: Do not cram: one long road day for every two or three rest days means fewer taxis.
Avoid Christmas–New Year and the May–June school holidays in Shimla and Manali.
Carry cash: ATMs in Kasol, Sangla and Chitkul run dry, and UPI fails on weak signal.
Skip paid snow points in winter; walk to snow above Old Manali or Shimla instead.
Agree taxi and guide prices before you start, including waiting time.

faqs.q: How much money do I need for 5 days in Himachal?
faqs.a: On a saver budget, plan ₹10,000–15,000 per person for 5 days from Delhi, including the return Volvo (₹3,000–3,800), hostel beds or shared doubles, dhaba meals and local buses. Add ₹2,000–4,000 if you want a paid trek guide, paragliding or more café meals.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to travel from Delhi to Himachal?
faqs.a: HRTC buses from Kashmere Gate ISBT. Ordinary buses are cheapest, while Volvos cost ₹1,300–1,900 one way to Manali or Dharamshala and are far more comfortable overnight. Sleeper-class trains to Kalka or Pathankot plus a local bus can be cheaper still.

faqs.q: Which is cheaper, Manali or Shimla?
faqs.a: For budget travellers, Manali and its villages are usually cheaper because of the many hostels and guesthouses in Old Manali and Vashisht. Shimla has fewer hostels and higher room rates near the Mall. Both are expensive in peak weeks.

Often, yes. HPTDC hotels are dependable, well located and fairly priced, with off-season discounts. Facilities are simple and service varies. Book on the HPTDC website and check current rates before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I travel Himachal on ₹1,000 a day?
faqs.a: Only with real effort: a dorm bed at ₹500, two dhaba meals and a short bus ride. It works for a few days in the off-season, but most travellers spend ₹1,800–3,000 a day once guides, entry fees and occasional taxis are counted.

faqs.q: Is it safe to stay in hostels in Himachal?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Established hostels have lockers, staff at night and women-only dorms. Read recent reviews, lock valuables, and in the Parvati valley stay alert to the drug scene and decline offers.

faqs.q: Do homestays in Himachal include meals?
faqs.a: Most homestays in Kinnaur, Tirthan and village areas include dinner and breakfast in the price, typically ₹1,200–2,500 per person. Confirm when you book, and tell hosts about dietary needs in advance.

faqs.q: When is the cheapest time to visit Himachal?
faqs.a: Late February to March, and from mid-October to early December outside Diwali, are good value: room rates fall and weather is often clear. July–August is cheap too, but monsoon landslides make it a poor time for road travel.

faqs.q: Do I need cash in Himachal?
faqs.a: Yes. UPI works in towns, but villages, buses and small dhabas may need cash, especially when signal drops. ATMs in Kasol, Sangla and Chitkul are unreliable; draw money in Manali, Kullu, Shimla, Dharamshala or Reckong Peo.
